Finding the exact word? No, it's not really like that. It's not that I'm standing there snapping my fingers trying to remember if it's called a 'pallet jack' or a 'hand truck.' I know the words. I’ll start off talking about the delivery trucks out back, making sure they get unloaded properly, but then suddenly I'm talking about Thursdays, and then before I know it I'm bringing up the church grill from the Sunday cookout, and then I'm going on about my boss’s tone of voice when he called me about the pallets last week. \n\nIt makes sense while I'm saying it, but I look at my employees and they just stand there holding their clipboards. They look at me like they absolutely can’t follow what I’m saying. They get these wide, blank eyes, like I lost them three sentences ago. And I try to backtrack to get us back to the inventory counts, but there's just so much I need to communicate to them and it all just keeps tangling together when I speak.\n\nDoctor: Have you been feeling unusually energized or high lately?\n\nPatient: Energized? High? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, if anything, it’s the exact opposite. I’m just... I'm exhausted, Doctor. You have to understand, running a retail floor at my age—I'm 59, you know—it takes a lot out of you even on a good day. You’re constantly on your feet, walking the aisles, checking the end-caps to make sure the corporate promotional displays are set up exactly to the planogram, dealing with vendors coming in the back door... \n\nAnd lately, with all this trouble I've been having, with my words getting all tangled up and the employees just staring at me like I'm speaking a foreign language, well, it's incredibly draining. It takes so much mental effort just to get through a simple ten-minute morning huddle now. I go home at the end of my shift and I just want to collapse in my recliner. There's no extra energy, no feeling revved up or on top of the world or anything like that. I wake up at 5:30 AM every single morning, I have my one cup of black coffee—same routine I've had since I got my degree, really—and I just try to push through the day. \n\nSo, no, definitely not energized. It's just a heavy, heavy feeling trying to keep the store running when I can't even get through the weekly numbers without my brain pulling my sentences in ten different directions. It just wears a person out.\n\nDoctor: Have you been hearing voices when no one else is around?\n\nPatient: Voices? Like... people talking when there's nobody there? No, Doctor, I haven't heard anything like that. The store is loud enough as it is, you know? Between the overhead music—which corporate insists on playing the exact same playlist every single day, I swear I hear those same twelve pop songs in my sleep—and the registers beeping, and the stockroom carts clattering over the tile floors, there's always noise. But it's all real noise, if you know what I mean. \n\nWhen I'm alone, like when I finally get home and sit down in my recliner... no, it's quiet. Well, I mean, the refrigerator hums, and sometimes I hear the neighbor's dog, but no voices. My problem isn't hearing things that aren't there, it's just... it's just getting the things that *are* in my head out of my mouth in an order that makes sense to my team. Like I was saying about the inventory counts, I know the numbers, I have the spreadsheets right there on my clipboard, but when I open my mouth to say \"we're short on the seasonal end-cap displays,\" it just spirals into something else entirely. But nobody is whispering to me or talking to me when I'm by myself, no. Just my own thoughts, getting tangled up.\n\nDoctor: Have you had a stroke or head injury recently?\n\nPatient: A stroke? Or a head injury? No, no, definitely nothing like that. I haven't hit my head, haven't been in any accidents. The last time I was in a hospital for anything physical was, oh, it must have been when I had my gallbladder taken out back in... well, that was a long time ago. But recently? No. \n\nI mean, I'm careful at work. We have strict safety protocols in the stockroom, you know, OSHA guidelines and all that. You can't just have people leaving pallets lying around or stacking boxes too high, especially the heavy liquid detergent boxes, those are a nightmare if they tip over. I always make sure the team is wearing their back braces if they're doing heavy lifting, and I certainly don't go climbing the tall ladders myself anymore, not at my age. We have the younger guys for that. \n\nAnd as for a stroke... well, I haven't had any of those warning signs they talk about on the television commercials, you know? My face isn't drooping, I can raise both my arms just fine, my vision hasn't gone blurry. I haven't collapsed or felt numb on one side. It's really just my speech, just the way my sentences get all scrambled up when I'm trying to direct the floor staff. It's not that my mouth isn't working, it's that the ideas just... they just run into each other. But physically, my head is perfectly fine. No bumps, no bruises, no strokes. Just a lot of frustration.\n\nDoctor: Have you started believing that people are trying to harm you or plot against you?\n\nPatient: Plotting against me? Harm me? No, Doctor, no, I don't think anyone is out to get me. I mean, retail is competitive, sure, and sometimes the district manager comes down hard on us if the shrink numbers are too high or if the payroll percentage creeps up past the target... but that's just business, you know? That's just the nature of the beast when you're managing a big box store. They want results, they want the shelves faced perfectly, they want the seasonal aisles flipped overnight from Halloween straight into Christmas, and they want it done with a skeleton crew. It's stressful, absolutely, and sometimes I feel like corporate is completely disconnected from the reality of what happens on the floor.\n\nBut as far as people actually trying to harm me? Or some kind of conspiracy against me personally? No, I don't feel that at all. The team I have, well, they're good kids mostly. A lot of college students working part-time, some older folks who just want to get out of the house. They get frustrated with me lately, sure, because of... well, because of what I've been telling you about, how my words just sort of derail when I'm trying to give them instructions. I can see it in their eyes, they get confused, maybe a little impatient when I start talking about the end-caps and suddenly I'm bringing up the pallet jack maintenance schedule in the middle of a sentence about promotional signage. But they aren't malicious. They aren't plotting anything. \n\nEven the vendors, the guys who deliver the soda and the chips, they can be pushy about getting prime shelf space, but that's just sales. Nobody is sneaking around trying to hurt me. My life is pretty simple, really. It's just the store, my recliner, my coffee... and this awful, awful trouble I'm having with my thoughts getting all jumbled up before they make it out of my mouth. But no, no plots, no enemies. Just a lot of confusion on my end.\n\nDoctor: Have you needed much less sleep than usual lately without feeling tired?\n\nPatient: Sleep? Needing less sleep? No, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, if anything, I feel like I could use more sleep, what with how exhausting the days have been lately. I mean, my sleep schedule is pretty set in stone, you know? I usually try to be in bed by 10:30, maybe 11:00 at the latest, right after the late local news. I like to catch the weather report because it really affects our foot traffic at the store—if they're calling for snow, even just a dusting, everybody rushes in for rock salt and milk, and I have to make sure the front end is staffed for the rush. \n\nSo I watch the news, I turn off the TV, and I'm usually up by 5:30 AM. My alarm goes off, and I have my routine. I make my coffee—just a standard drip maker, none of those fancy pod machines, I like the smell of the grounds in the morning—and I sit in my recliner for about twenty minutes just to wake up before I get in the shower. I get my solid six and a half, maybe seven hours most nights. And I definitely feel it if I don't. \n\nLike last week, the overnight crew had an issue with the alarm system—the motion sensor by the receiving doors kept tripping, and the monitoring company called me at 2:00 in the morning. By the time I got it sorted out over the phone with the shift lead and finally got back to sleep, it was almost 3:30. When my alarm went off at 5:30, I was dragging. I felt it all day long. I had to drink three cups of coffee in the breakroom just to keep my eyes open while I was trying to review the shrink report, and even then, my head felt heavy. So no, I definitely don't have that thing where I don't need sleep. I need it, and I'm tired just like anybody else if I don't get enough of it. It's just... the exhaustion makes the talking worse, I think. When I'm tired, the words get even more tangled up. But my sleep itself, the amount I need, that hasn't changed at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you been having trouble understanding what other people say to you?\n\nPatient: Understanding other people? Oh, no, no trouble with that at all. My hearing is fine, and my comprehension is perfectly fine. I know exactly what everyone is saying to me. When the district manager calls and tells me we need to push the loyalty program harder because our store's sign-up rate dropped by two percent last quarter, I understand him loud and clear. When the cashiers tell me their registers are out of receipt paper, or a customer comes up to me looking for the automotive section, I know exactly what they want. \n\nIt's actually very frustrating, you see, because I take in the information perfectly. I process it. Someone asks me a question, say, about where we moved the clearance items, and in my head, the answer is right there. I know they're on the back wall near the seasonal department. I understand their question completely. But then, when I open my mouth to tell them, the words that come out... well, they just aren't the ones I meant to say. Or they are, but they're mixed in with thoughts about the inventory sheets or the squeaky wheel on the flatbed cart I was just pushing. \n\nSo the problem isn't coming in, it's going out. I'm taking everything in just fine. I read the company memos, I listen to the morning huddle, I hear the complaints about the breakroom refrigerator smelling like old tuna—which, by the way, I've asked them to clean out every Friday, but nobody ever does—and I understand all of it. Every single word. It's just my own words that are betraying me. So, no, understanding people isn't an issue at all. I just wish they could understand me as well as I understand them.\n\nDoctor: Have you had any seizures recently?\n\nPatient: Seizures? No, no. I've never had a seizure. Not recently, not ever in my fifty-nine years. I mean, physically, I'm actually in pretty decent shape, all things considered. You know, working retail, you're on your feet all day. Those concrete floors with just that thin layer of commercial tile over them—they absolutely destroy your knees and your lower back over the years. I've got a bit of stiffness, sure, and sometimes if I'm helping unload a truck because the receiving department is short-staffed again, I'll definitely feel it the next morning in my lumbar. I take an ibuprofen and I'm fine. But seizures? No. \n\nLike, falling down and convulsing? Never. We actually had an incident at the store, oh, it must have been three or four years ago now, right before the Thanksgiving rush. A customer had a seizure right in the middle of the baking aisle. Aisle four. She just completely collapsed, knocked over a whole display of condensed milk and pie crusts. It was terrifying, to be completely honest with you. I had to sprint over there, we called 911 immediately, and I had my shift lead block off both ends of the aisle with shopping carts so people wouldn't crowd around her, and we just tried to make sure she didn't hit her head on the metal base decks of the shelving until the paramedics arrived. \n\nSo I know what a seizure looks like, and I know how serious they can be. But no, I haven't had anything even remotely like that happen to me. My body works just fine, my heart is good, my blood pressure is usually fine... it's really just, well, like I was saying before, it's just the words that get all scrambled up on the way out. My brain doesn't shut down or make me shake or pass out or anything physical like that. Just the talking. So, no, definitely no seizures.\n\nDoctor: Do you often have trouble finding the exact word you want to say?\n\nPatient: Finding the exact word? No, it's not really like that. My vocabulary is perfectly fine, I've got a bachelor's degree in business administration, I know how to speak. \n\nIt's more like... well, like I was saying before, it's not that I can't find the word, it's that the wrong ones come out with it, or they all come out at once. Suddenly? No, no, it wasn't like a light switch flipping off, or on, I suppose. It wasn't like I woke up one Tuesday and suddenly couldn't give Dave a straight instruction about the endcaps. It's been more of a... a gradual slide, I guess you could say. Like a slow leak in a tire. You don't notice it right away, but eventually, you're driving on the rim. 

I'd say it's been going on for about six months now. That's when I really started noticing it, or at least, that's when it became impossible to ignore. Because before that, maybe I'd have a little slip of the tongue, or I'd lose my train of thought for a second—which happens to everyone, right? Especially when you're managing a floor with twenty different things happening at once. But about six months ago, that's when the jumbled explanations really started. I'd be trying to explain the new return policy to a customer—corporate changed it from thirty days to forty-five, but only with a receipt, and only for certain departments, which is a nightmare to enforce, let me tell you—and I'd just start throwing in things about the floor buffer being broken or the delivery truck being delayed at the distribution center. 

And then there are the stops. The odd stops. I'll just be walking across the sales floor, heading from the backroom to the customer service desk to approve a void, and I'll just... stop. Right in the middle of the main action alley. And it's not because I saw a spill that needed cleaning or a display that was knocked over. I just stop because the words and the thoughts are all crashing together in my head, and I have to physically halt just to try and sort them out. It's been about half a year of this. Six months of people looking at me like I've grown a second head while I stand there in front of the seasonal aisle trying to untangle my own sentences. So, no, definitely not sudden. Just a slow, incredibly frustrating build-up over the last six months.
